(Mary Conlon/AP) Editor's Note: This story was featured in WBUR's weekly health newsletter, CommonHealth. If you like what you read and want it in your inbox, sign up here. As measles surges in the United States at the highest level in decades, doctors and public health officials are warning Massachusetts could be vulnerable to an outbreak. While 96.5% of the state's kindergarteners had received measles vaccines as of last school year, state data shows some counties dipped below the 95% threshold considered essential for herd immunity, making their students more vulnerable to infections. So far this year, two cases of measles have been recorded in Massachusetts. But Dr. David Lyczkowski, president of the Massachusetts chapter of the American Academy of Pediatrics, said he’s watching the outbreak a couple states away in Pennsylvania, and he’s concerned. “It is a roll of the dice,” he said. “I'm worried that it's just a matter of time before we see an outbreak.” Registered nurse Danielle Capuano prepares a vaccine at Hyde Park Pediatrics. (Jesse Costa/WBUR) Vaccination rates vary widely across communities and schools. Many schools are at 100% — meaning every kindergarten student is up to date on vaccines. But in some others, 1 out of 5 has not received their measles shots, according to data from the state Department of Public Health reviewed by WBUR. The numbers include the 2025-2026 school year; data for the current school year is not yet available. Support WBUR In Franklin County in Western Massachusetts, 89.7% of kindergarteners had received their measles shots. On Martha’s Vineyard, the vaccination rate for measles was 91.2%. And in the more populous Suffolk County, which includes Boston, the rate was 94.2% — an improvement compared with prior years, but still below the 95% threshold needed to guard against the spread of the virus. “The number of classrooms that are out there that could be the site of the next measles outbreak — it's really alarming,” Lyczkowski said. Across the country, measles has appeared in almost every state and is spreading more rapidly than it did last year. By the beginning of October, there were 3,887 confirmed cases in the United States this year, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention — the vast majority in people who are unvaccinated. The biggest outbreak in decades is now unfolding in Pennsylvania, where state officials have tracked over 1,000 cases and five deaths associated with the disease. “With soaring measles activity in the U.S. and abroad, it is likely that measles will be introduced into Massachusetts,” said Ann Scales, a spokesperson for the state Department of Public Health. “We are fortunate to have an overall very high rate of measles vaccination in Massachusetts but acknowledge that there are undervaccinated pockets where an outbreak of limited size could occur.” She said if there are suspected cases of measles in Massachusetts, state officials work with healthcare providers to identify and isolate infected people as quickly as possible. Meanwhile, pediatricians say, vaccine hesitancy is on the rise, fueled at least in part by statements from President Trump and Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. questioning the safety of routine childhood vaccines, despite decades of evidence that they are safe and effective, and save lives. In August, Trump signed an executive order promoting fewer vaccines for children, and advocating to break up the measles, mumps and rubella, or MMR, vaccine into three separate shots — which currently don’t exist in the U.S. Support WBUR These kinds of statements often come up during patient visits at Dr. Jonathan Schwab’s office in Northampton. “ It definitely has an effect on people either making their decisions — or certainly questioning the recommendations that I suggest,” said Schwab, a pediatrician for over 35 years. “When you hear people who are in a high position in our country say things that are incorrect, even if you know that they're incorrect, it starts to make you worried,” he said. “I think that's just human nature.” (Map courtesy Massachusetts Department of Public Health) Vaccines are not always easy to access — families who live in rural areas face greater challenges getting medical care than people who live in more populated areas. And studies suggest families in rural areas are more likely to question the importance of vaccines. Statewide, the number of parents choosing not to vaccinate their children for religious reasons has been ticking upward since the COVID-19 pandemic. In Massachusetts, 1,169 kindergarten students had religious exemptions last year, representing 1.6% of children statewide. That’s up from fewer than 700 children in 2020. In Franklin County, more than 5% of kindergarten students had religious exemptions, and nearly 8% were out of compliance — meaning they had no exemption and hadn’t submitted records to show proof of vaccination. Nationally, too, more families are seeking exemptions, and vaccination rates are falling. The CDC reports 92.4% of U.S. kindergarteners had received measles vaccines in the last school year. Pediatricians recommend two doses of the MMR vaccine for full protection, with the first shot given at age 1 and the second between ages 4 and 6. Dr. Elisabeth DiPietro at Hyde Park Pediatrics. She encourages families to get the measles vaccine. (Jesse Costa/WBUR) Dr. Elisabeth DiPietro urges her patients to get all their vaccines when they’re due, especially — right now — the MMR vaccine. Support WBUR When a person with measles passes through a room, infectious particles can remain in the air for hours. Nine out of 10 unvaccinated people who come in contact with the virus will catch it. “It is very contagious,” DiPietro said. The virus causes fever and rash, and can lead to serious long-term health problems, particularly for young children who are not immunized. In some cases, measles can lead to blindness, brain damage or death. DiPietro, a pediatrician in Hyde Park, said she was among a group of college students who got sick with measles during an outbreak in 1987, even though she had received one dose of vaccine. She said that experience showed her just how quickly the virus can spread. As for whether measles could show up in Massachusetts again, DiPietro says: “It’s not if — it’s when.” “It'll be lucky or unlucky whether or not the virus happens to travel through Western Mass. or Dukes County,” she said, noting the lower vaccination rates in those areas. DiPietro said over the past two years, she’s noticed a big increase in hesitancy among her patients. She said more families are asking questions and raising concerns about vaccines. “Families really struggle when they're getting conflicting advice and information from the CDC, from the health secretary, and from the president, that's really in conflict with their primary care pediatrician that they've known and trusted for years,” she said. “There’s just so much confusion and chaos.” This segment aired on October 6, 2026. The clinic offered free MMR vaccinations as the South Carolina Department of Health reported 876 cases of measles earlier in the week, most centered in Spartanburg County. (Sean Rayford/Getty Images/TNS) (Sean Rayford/Getty Images North America/ / Tribune News Service) Add Spokesman-Review on Google By Tim Henderson Stateline.org Measles cases for the calendar year surpassed 4,000 for the first time in decades, with as many as five deaths in Pennsylvania, as the federal government steps in with financial help for states but also fans vaccination fears and skepticism. A weekly report from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention showed 4,080 cases this year as of Thursday, up 192 cases in a week. Pennsylvania, which has reported five confirmed deaths from measles, alone had 142 new cases for the week – for a total of 1,105 for the year. The CDC has recognized just two of the state’s reported deaths. Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, a Democrat, has protested the CDC’s death count; his state’s five deaths would be more than the three deaths reported in 2025 for the entire nation. Other states with large numbers of cases, more than 200, did not see their case numbers change for the week: South Carolina (670 for the year), Utah (535) and Wisconsin (207). States with more cases included New York, which declared a measles emergency, with 19 new cases for a total of 103 this year; and Iowa, up 17 cases to 39. Kentucky reported separately on Friday that cases there had reached 104, up 10 from last week. Pennsylvania, which has become ground zero for this year’s outbreaks, reported this week that a new awareness and pop-up vaccine clinics are leading to more measles vaccinations. All but five states have had at least one measles case this year. The last time the United States had this many cases was in 1991, reaching 9,643 cases as the nation still struggled to roll out vaccinations for the disease, amid budget cuts that hit programs in big cities. Pennsylvania’s health department this week announced “a surge of interest” in vaccinations as more residents become aware of the outbreak – more than 56,000 doses were given out in September, more than twice the usual monthly volume. The state has added pop-up clinics in the most affected areas. All but four of the measles cases were among unvaccinated people. The Lewistown Sentinel reported that an 18-year-old woman there died in September from brain swelling as a result of the measles virus after two of her brothers survived the disease. While the federal government has offered states more funding to combat measles, Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy moved forward this week on plans to emphasize vaccine injury, announcing a new clinic and work to strengthen a database that tracks problems after a vaccination. “We must listen to patients and families who report vaccine injuries – not dismiss or gaslight them,” Kennedy said in a statement. ✕

Health officials say the infected person is recovering at home while investigators trace potential exposures in the community. Health officials say the measles virus spreads through the air when an infected person coughs, sneezes, or even breathes, and can remain in the air for up to an hour after that person leaves an area. Pennsylvania health officials said on Monday the state's total had passed 1,000 cases, making it the largest state outbreak in more than three decades. The US is having its worst year for measles since 1991, with nearly 3,900 cases reported, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The order allows registered nurses to order tests for suspected measles and pharmacists to vaccinate children as young as two. It also requires all MMR vaccinations to be reported to state or New York City immunisation registries within 72 hours, while waiving adults' consent for such reporting. Vaccination itself still requires the consent of the patient or a legal guardian. The emergency took effect on Monday and runs through November 4. Kathy Hochul has declared a state disaster emergency over the growing number of measles cases across rural areas of New York. She said this enables the state to respond more swiftly to the outbreak and allows healthcare professionals to take additional steps to get more New Yorkers vaccinated and tested, if needed. “No one should get seriously ill or die from a vaccine-preventable disease,” said Hochul. “That is why I have taken steps to increase the number of health professionals who can vaccinate and test. These emergency measures will protect New Yorkers and support our community partners as they work tirelessly to address the spread of this disease.” Case numbers As of Oct. 3, there have been seven confirmed cases in New York City and 101 in the rest of the state, for 108 total cases this year, amid a global and domestic increase in measles cases. Lewis County has had 11 people test positive for measles. None of them had been vaccinated. Vaccine The state says the MMR vaccine is highly effective and is the best protection against measles. Most people born before 1957 are considered immune because they were likely exposed to the virus. Those who received the vaccine between 1963 and 1967 may have received a vaccine that wasn’t as effective and should talk to their health care provider about getting revaccinated. Since July 15, local health departments have administered more than 1,000 doses of the MMR vaccine across rural areas of New York state. Measles symptoms and complications Measles is a highly contagious respiratory disease that causes rash and fever. In some cases, measles can reduce the immune system’s ability to fight other infections like pneumonia. The disease is caused by a virus spread by coughing or sneezing into the air. People can catch the disease by breathing in the virus or, less commonly, by touching a contaminated surface, then touching the eyes, nose or mouth. Serious complications of measles include hospitalization, pneumonia, miscarriage, preterm birth, brain swelling, immune amnesia and death. Long-term complications can include subacute sclerosing panencephalitis, a type of brain inflammation resulting from an earlier measles infection that can lead to permanent brain damage years after the initial infection. records.content: 24/7 LiveNew York CityNew JerseyLong IslandNorthern SuburbsConnecticut 64° HEALTH & FITNESS Hochul declares state disaster emergency over ongoing measles outbreak Monday, October 5, 2026 6:51PM Stream New York's #1 news - AccuWeather - original content 24/7 NEW YORK (WABC) -- Governor Kathy Hochul has issued an executive order on Monday declaring a State Disaster Emergency in response to the growing number of measles cases across rural areas of New York and neighboring states. As of October 3, there have been seven confirmed cases in New York City and 101 in New York State outside of of the city, for 108 total cases this year, amid a global and domestic increase in measles cases. Since July 15, there have been 92 cases reported among under-immunized, rural communities in 18 counties. Since then, local health departments have administered over 1,000 doses of the MMR vaccine across rural areas of New York State. The executive order signed on Monday expands the network of vaccine administrators to add paramedics, advanced EMS, midwives and pharmacists. "After reviewing the latest data on measles cases in New York State, I am declaring a State Disaster Emergency to strengthen our ongoing efforts to confront this disease," Governor Hochul said. "No one should get seriously ill or die from a vaccine-preventable disease. That is why I have taken steps to increase the number of health professionals who can vaccinate and test. These emergency measures will protect New Yorkers and support our community partners as they work tirelessly to address the spread of this disease." The governor received her flu shot on Monday and is urging all New Yorkers to do the same. New York Governor Kathy Hochul speaks during a news conference, Friday, Oct. 2, 2026, in New York. records.content: Wellness Measles cases surpass 1,000 in Pennsylvania amid the state's largest outbreak in decades 1:08 Measles cases surpass 1,000 in Pennsylvania Measles cases surpass 1,000 in Pennsylvania By Mary Kekatos October 05, 2026, 6:48 PM Measles cases in Pennsylvania have surpassed 1,000 so far this year as the state continues to battle its largest outbreak in decades. Monday's update from the Pennsylvania Department of Health (DOH) brings the total number of 2026 measles cases in the state to 1,004 across 39 counties. At least 198 people have been hospitalized, and five measles-associated deaths have been reported, DOH data shows. Related Articles An infant is one of the 2 measles-associated deaths in Pennsylvania Two of the deaths were among unvaccinated adults: an 18-year-old and a 40-year-old. The other two deaths were among infants who were too young to have received the measles, mumps, rubella (MMR) vaccine. The fifth death occurred in an unvaccinated resident of Lancaster County, in southeastern Pennsylvania, but it is unclear how old the individual is. Lancaster County is the epicenter of the state's outbreak, with 391 cases confirmed so far. Fewer than 1% of the state's cases are among those who are fully vaccinated with the MMR vaccine, according to DOH. Measles virus particle, illustration. Kateryna Kon/science Photo Library/Getty Images Last week, following confirmation of the fifth death by the Pennsylvania health department, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) told ABC News in a statement it was "deeply saddened to hear of another death" in the state. "Under Secretary [Robert F.] Kennedy's leadership, CDC has mounted an aggressive response to measles outbreaks across the country. Texas, South Carolina, Virginia, Kansas, New Mexico, and Wisconsin requested CDC Epi-Aids and worked alongside federal teams to help bring their outbreaks rapidly and successfully under control," the statement read. "CDC has not received a formal Epi-Aid request from Pennsylvania. If requested, CDC stands ready to deploy epidemiologists to support the state's identified needs," the statement continued. A CDC Epi-Aid is a rapid, short-term field investigation from the federal health agency of an "urgent public health problem." The Epi-Aid provides resources such as, but not limited to, increasing the workforce available for rapid response and building epidemiologic capacity, according to the CDC . Meanwhile, measles cases in the U.S. have surpassed 3,800 so far in 2026, with cases confirmed in 45 states and Washington, D.C., according to the latest data from the CDC. It's the highest number of illnesses since 1991. Related Articles How hospitals, clinics in Pennsylvania are responding to the measles outbreak The CDC currently recommends that people receive two doses of the MMR vaccine, the first at ages 12 to 15 months and the second between 4 and 6 years old. One dose is 93% effective in preventing measles infection and two doses are 97% effective, the CDC says. Infants aged 6 to 11 months living in or traveling to high-risk outbreak areas may receive an early third dose of the MMR vaccine. However, CDC data shows vaccination rates have been lagging in recent years. During the 2025 to 2026 school year, 92.4% of kindergartners received the MMR vaccine, according to data. This is lower than the 95.2% seen in the 2019 to 2020 school year, prior to the COVID-19 pandemic. In Pennsylvania, more than 8,800 doses of the MMR vaccine have been administered by DOH staff. Of those doses, about 3,500 were administered in August and more than 2,500 were administered in September. ABC News' Youri Benadjaoud contributed to this report. CTV’s Kimberley Fowler reports. Ottawa Public Health (OPH) is alerting residents to several possible measles exposure locations in connection with two confirmed infections in the city. In a news release on Thursday, OPH said the two residents were exposed to measles outside Ontario. Health workers are reaching out directly to people who might have been exposed but are issuing a public notice in order to reach individuals who may have been exposed but could not be contacted directly or whose contact information was incomplete or unavailable. “At this time, the risk to the general population remains low,” OPH says. Ottawa Public Health says individuals who visited the following locations in Ottawa, on the dates and times below, may have been exposed to the measles virus: Tim Hortons at 3224 Hawthorne Rd. When: Thursday, Oct. 1 between 5:30 and 8 p.m. (Monitor until Thursday, Oct. 22) Your Independent Grocer at 1910 St. Laurent Blvd. When: Friday, Oct. 2 between 3:15 and 5:45 p.m. (Monitor until Friday, Oct. 23) Rexall Drugstore at 1910 St. Laurent Blvd. When: Friday, Oct. 2 between 3:45 and 6 p.m. (Monitor until Friday, Oct. 23) Metro Supermarket at 2261 Walkley Rd. When: Friday, Oct. 2 between 4 and 6:15 p.m. (Monitor until Friday, Oct. 23) Subway at 3190 Hawthorne Rd. When: Friday, Oct. 2 between 5:30 and 8 p.m. (Monitor until Friday, Oct. 23) McDonalds at 1796 St. Laurent Blvd. When: Friday, Oct. 2 between 5:30 and 8 p.m. (Monitor until Friday, Oct. 23) Ruby’s Restaurant at 10 York St. When: Friday, Oct. 2 between 6:30 and 9:30 p.m. (Monitor until Friday, Oct. 23) Tim Hortons at 2800 Lancaster Rd. When: Saturday, Oct. 3 between 5:30 and 8 p.m. (Monitor until Saturday, Oct. 24) Individuals who attended the above locations during the specified times may have been exposed to the measles virus and are asked to monitor for symptoms for 21 days from the date of exposure, even if vaccinated, and to check vaccination records to confirm a previous vaccination. “The measles vaccine is typically noted as ‘MMR’, ‘MMRV’ or ‘M’ on records. Most children in Ontario receive two doses of measles vaccine by age seven based on the current routine vaccine schedule: one at 12 months of age and another between four to six years of age,” OPH says. “People born before 1970 likely had measles in the past and are generally considered immune (protected).” If you develop symptoms, call your health care provider and notify them of your recent measles exposure. If you do not have a health care provider, please visit Health811 or call 8-1-1 to connect with a registered nurse for free, secure and confidential health advice. Symptoms of measles Measles is a highly contagious viral respiratory infection caused by the measles virus. Symptoms include high fever, cough, runny nose, white spots in the mouth, and red watery eyes that may be sensitive to light and can appear up to 21 days after exposure but usually occur within seven to 12 days. A few days after symptoms begin, a red rash usually develops that starts on the face and spreads down the body to the arms and legs. This rash usually lasts four to seven days. Symptoms generally last from one to two weeks. (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention / AP) The first measles case in an Allegheny County resident was reported by the Allegheny County Health Department late Monday afternoon. The county said that anyone who visited the Target at Pine Creek Shopping Center in McCandless (9805 McKnight Road) on Thursday, Oct. 1 between 3:45 and 5:45 p.m. may have been exposed to the person with measles The infected person, who is unvaccinated and under 18, is recovering at home. The county said that no school exposures have resulted from this case. The health department said unvaccinated people concerned about being exposed Oct. 1 at the Target should call a healthcare provider right away. The announcement emphasized that people should “not go directly to a healthcare facility without calling ahead.” Two doses of the MMR (measles-mumps-rubella) vaccine are recommended, the county said. People who have had only one dose “may still be susceptible to the virus.” A highly contagious virus, measles spreads “when an infected person breaths, coughs or sneezes. The virus remains in the air and on surfaces for up to two hours, even after the infected person leaves the area.” The Allegheny County Health Department provides free vaccines to people without health insurance. The Immunization Clinic is at 425 First Ave. in Downtown Pittsburgh. Call 412-578-8062 to make an appointment and click here for details. The county noted “there is no risk in getting an additional dose of the MMR vaccine for individuals who are uncertain but may have already received it.”

Officials say the new case is connected to the first case, reported earlier this week. The Health Department says the cases are connected because both patients go to the same school “which suggests there was likely a previously unknown exposure at the school.” The Post-Gazette reports the school is Eden Christian Academy in the North Hills.
